The irony is that OKR's inventor operated in one of the least error-tolerant, longest-cycle businesses—semiconductors—yet the version exported to China was shaped by internet-era assumptions about rapid iteration and tolerated failure.

The article argues the real variable is not industry but recoverability of failure. Some decisions—building production lines, tooling, tape-out, locking supply chains—are irreversible once committed. Hard tech therefore leans toward Stage-Gate and IPD gate reviews, where progress is gated by evidence rather than pulled by aspirational targets. When hard-tech firms adopt OKR, frontline teams spontaneously translate it into delivery metrics—a correction by reality, not execution drift. The article cites a chip-company case where scoring was re-linked to annual performance, precisely what classic OKR forbids, and KRs phrased as committed deliverables (e.g., launch three new products, obtain two patents).
